body:
Two kinds of territories before Independence

When India became independent on 15 August 1947, the new government faced a major problem: the territories of pre-Independence India did not form a single, directly administered political unit. They consisted of British Indian provinces and numerous princely states.

British Indian provinces were governed directly under British authority. Princely states, by contrast, were ruled by hereditary rulers such as maharajas and nawabs. These rulers generally controlled their internal administration but accepted British supremacy in important matters.

British paramountcy

British paramountcy, also called British suzerainty, was the superior authority exercised by the British Crown over the princely states. The states retained varying degrees of internal autonomy but were not fully independent of British control.

What changed in August 1947?

The Indian Independence Act, 1947 provided for the creation of the independent Dominions of India and Pakistan. It also ended British paramountcy over the princely states. The political relationship that had connected their rulers to the British Crown therefore came to an end.

British policy left the rulers to decide whether their states would join India, join Pakistan or seek a separate existence. This created a serious danger of political fragmentation. Large princely territories lay between British-administered provinces, while numerous smaller states interrupted the geographical continuity of the country.

NCERT Class 12 Political Science refers to 565 princely states. GCERT Class 8 Social Science describes the number as approximately 562. These textbook figures should not be treated as identical; the essential historical issue was the integration of several hundred differently administered territories.

Why integration was necessary

A newly independent country needed a common authority capable of protecting its territory, conducting foreign relations and maintaining essential communications. If numerous princely states remained separate, transport routes, defence arrangements and relations between neighbouring territories could become difficult to manage.

Integration also had a democratic purpose. Many princely states had limited representative government, while their populations increasingly demanded participation in public affairs. Bringing these territories into the Indian Union created the conditions for common constitutional institutions and more accountable administration.

Integration was therefore not simply the collection of signatures from rulers. It involved bringing territories under a shared political framework and, subsequently, reorganising their administration.

Prelims focus

  • India became independent on 15 August 1947.
  • The Indian Independence Act, 1947 ended British paramountcy over princely states.
  • British Indian provinces were directly administered; princely states had hereditary rulers under British paramountcy.
  • NCERT Class 12 refers to 565 princely states; GCERT Class 8 gives approximately 562.
  • Trap: The end of British paramountcy did not automatically place every princely state under the direct administration of the Indian government.

[NCERT, Class 12, Political Science, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 14–16; NCERT, Class 8, History, Our Pasts–III, Chapter 10, India After Independence, printed p. 128; GCERT, Class 8, Social Science, Gujarati edition, Chapter 8, India: Post Independence, section on integration of princely states.]

title: The Challenge of Uniting Princely India in 1947

body:
The principal leaders of integration

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the first Home Minister and Deputy Prime Minister of independent India, played the leading political role in persuading princely rulers to join the Indian Union. He combined firmness about national unity with assurances intended to reduce the rulers' fears.

V. P. Menon, a senior administrator associated with the States Department, worked closely with Patel. He helped conduct negotiations and prepare the legal and administrative arrangements through which accession and subsequent mergers were implemented.

The States Department was established on 5 July 1947. On that date, Patel publicly invited the princely states to join India in matters of common national concern. Lord Mountbatten, then the Crown Representative, also encouraged rulers to accede and addressed a special meeting of princes on 25 July 1947.

Accession initially concerned 3 essential subjects

The initial arrangement did not require rulers to surrender every responsibility of government. Instead, the standard Instrument of Accession transferred authority to the Dominion of India over 3 principal subjects:

  • Defence: Matters concerning the armed forces and protection against external threats.
  • External affairs: Relations with foreign countries and related international matters.
  • Communications: Important services such as posts, telegraphs, railways and major transport communications.

The Instrument also covered specified matters ancillary to these subjects. Other aspects of internal government generally remained with the ruler under the initial arrangement. The ruler executed the Instrument, and the Governor-General accepted it on behalf of the Dominion.

Accession, standstill and merger were different arrangements

ArrangementMain purposeImportant distinction
Instrument of AccessionCreated a constitutional relationship with the Indian Dominion on specified subjects.Did not, by itself, abolish the ruler's internal administration.
Standstill AgreementTemporarily continued existing administrative arrangements and services.Continuity of services was not the same as political accession.
Merger AgreementTransferred governing authority and administration to the Indian government or another agreed authority.Went beyond the limited initial accession arrangement.
Union CovenantCombined several princely states into one larger political and administrative unit.Created a common government for the participating states.

These instruments often operated at different stages. A ruler could first accede on the essential subjects and later agree to merge the state's administration with a province or a newly formed union of states.

How Patel and Menon secured cooperation

The policy relied primarily on negotiation and persuasion. Patel emphasised the practical need for unity, while Menon helped translate political agreements into workable legal documents. Assurances concerning internal autonomy during initial accession, and arrangements for rulers' personal privileges and privy purses (annual payments to rulers) during later mergers, helped obtain consent.

Geography also mattered. States lying within or adjoining the territory of the Indian Dominion were encouraged to establish a common relationship with it. Most such princely states agreed to accede before Independence. However, Junagadh, Hyderabad and Jammu and Kashmir presented particularly difficult situations.

A distinction that prevents many errors

Accession established the constitutional link. Merger or a union covenant could subsequently transfer or combine administrative authority. These were related but not identical steps.

Prelims focus

  • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: Deputy Prime Minister and first Home Minister.
  • V. P. Menon: Senior administrator and key participant in negotiations and documentation.
  • 5 July 1947: Establishment of the States Department and Patel's appeal to princely states.
  • 25 July 1947: Mountbatten addressed a special meeting of princes.
  • Instrument of Accession: Defence, external affairs and communications were the 3 principal subjects.
  • Trap: A Standstill Agreement was not automatically an Instrument of Accession.

[Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States (1950), Part 4, paragraphs 76–82 and Appendices V, VI, VII and IX, online transcription consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, Political Science, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed p. 16.]

pictures.alt: The 1947 negotiations led to accession on specified subjects while internal administration generally remained with rulers; later agreements could change administration.
pictures.caption: The accession policy first established a common authority for defence, external affairs and communications.

title: Patel, Menon and the Legal Steps to Integration

body:
Why Junagadh became a difficult case

Junagadh was a princely state in the Kathiawar region of present-day Gujarat. Its population was predominantly Hindu, while its ruler was a Muslim Nawab, Mahabat Khanji III.

In 1947, the Nawab decided to accede to Pakistan. This was controversial because Junagadh was surrounded by territory associated with India and lacked a land boundary with Pakistan. Most neighbouring princely states in Kathiawar had chosen to join India.

The ruler's decision was therefore opposed by many people in Junagadh and the surrounding region. It became a significant test of whether the political choice of a princely ruler would be accepted when it conflicted with the wishes expressed by much of the local population.

The Arzi Hukumat and the transfer of administration

In September 1947, opponents of the Nawab's decision established the Arzi Hukumat, or provisional government, in Bombay. It was led by Samaldas Gandhi and supported the demand for Junagadh to join India.

As the political and administrative situation deteriorated, the Nawab left for Pakistan. Representatives acting for the state requested that the Government of India take over its administration. On 9 November 1947, the Indian government assumed administrative control of Junagadh.

This date marks the Indian government's takeover of administration. It should not be confused with the later public vote or Junagadh's subsequent administrative incorporation into Saurashtra.

The public vote and later incorporation into Saurashtra

A plebiscite is a direct vote in which the population expresses its choice on an important political question. A plebiscite concerning Junagadh's accession was held on 20 February 1948. An overwhelming majority of the votes cast supported joining India.

Junagadh's integration did not end with this vote. In December 1948, its elected representatives supported transferring administration to the neighbouring Saurashtra government. The Government of Saurashtra took over Junagadh's administration on 20 January 1949.

Three events, three different meanings

  • 9 November 1947: Government of India assumed administration.
  • 20 February 1948: A plebiscite strongly supported joining India.
  • 20 January 1949: Saurashtra government assumed administration.

These are not interchangeable accession, voting and merger dates.

Prelims focus

  • Junagadh: Princely state in Kathiawar, now part of Gujarat.
  • Mahabat Khanji III: Nawab who chose accession to Pakistan in 1947.
  • Samaldas Gandhi: Leader of the Arzi Hukumat established in Bombay.
  • 9 November 1947: Indian government took over administration.
  • 20 February 1948: Plebiscite overwhelmingly favoured India.
  • Trap: Junagadh's transfer to Saurashtra took place in January 1949, not immediately after the February 1948 vote.

[NCERT, Class 12, Political Science, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed p. 16; GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Gujarati edition, Chapter 7, Post-Independence India, section on Junagadh; Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States (1950), Part 11, The Position of Junagadh State, paragraph 223, printed pp. 113–114, online transcription consulted 22 November 2026; Nirupama Subramanian, The Indian Express, Explained: When Junagadh voted to join India, 5 August 2020, sections on Junagadh's accession and plebiscite, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Residents in period Kathiawar clothing queue outside a modest public building to vote in Junagadh's February 1948 plebiscite.
pictures.caption: The February 1948 plebiscite registered strong public support for Junagadh joining India.

pictures.alt: Timeline separating India's administrative takeover in 1947, the February 1948 plebiscite and Saurashtra's administrative takeover in January 1949.

title: Junagadh: From the Nawab's Decision to the 1948 Plebiscite

body:
Hyderabad's position in 1947

Hyderabad was the largest princely state and was situated in the Deccan, surrounded by Indian territory. Its ruler was known as the Nizam. Although the state had a predominantly Hindu population, the ruling establishment was headed by the Muslim Nizam.

Unlike most neighbouring princely states, Hyderabad's ruler sought an independent position rather than immediate accession to India. Its location in the middle of the Indian subcontinent made this particularly difficult for the new Indian government.

The Standstill Agreement

In November 1947, Hyderabad and India entered into a Standstill Agreement. The arrangement was intended to maintain existing administrative relationships while the parties continued negotiations about Hyderabad's political future.

A standstill arrangement helped prevent an immediate breakdown of services and official dealings. It did not mean that Hyderabad had acceded to India.

Popular opposition and the Razakars

Opposition to the Nizam's rule increased within Hyderabad. The Hyderabad State Congress demanded political change, while peasants in the Telangana region participated in a movement against oppressive conditions. Communist organisations played an important role in the peasant struggle.

The Nizam's government relied in part on an armed organisation called the Razakars. Its activities included intimidation and serious violence. These developments worsened the conflict between the Hyderabad administration, its opponents and the Government of India.

Operation Polo and Hyderabad's integration

After negotiations failed to resolve the crisis, India undertook a military operation officially described at the time as a police action. The operation was known as Operation Polo.

Indian forces entered Hyderabad on 13 September 1948. The operation led to the Nizam's surrender and a ceasefire on 17 September 1948. Hyderabad subsequently came under Indian authority and was integrated into the Indian constitutional framework.

Why the term police action can be misleading

Operation Polo was carried out by the Indian armed forces. Its description as a police action does not mean that it was an ordinary operation conducted only by civilian police.

How Hyderabad differed from Junagadh

Junagadh's case involved the Nawab's decision to join Pakistan, the Indian takeover of administration and a subsequent public plebiscite. Hyderabad's case involved a ruler seeking independence, a Standstill Agreement, major internal political conflict and the military operation of September 1948.

The two cases demonstrate that India did not use one identical method in every princely state. The circumstances of each territory influenced the form of intervention and subsequent integration.

Prelims focus

  • Hyderabad: Largest princely state, surrounded by Indian territory.
  • Nizam: Title of Hyderabad's ruler, who initially sought independence.
  • November 1947: Standstill Agreement with India.
  • Razakars: Armed organisation associated with the Nizam's rule.
  • 13–17 September 1948: Operation Polo; the Nizam surrendered on 17 September.
  • Trap: Operation Polo was a military operation, not Junagadh's plebiscite.

[NCERT, Class 12, Political Science, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 17–18; GCERT, Class 8, Social Science, Gujarati edition, Chapter 8, India: Post Independence, section on Hyderabad; Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States (1950), Part 11, Establishment of Constitutional Relationship with Hyderabad State, paragraph 222, online transcription consulted 22 November 2026; Ministry of Home Affairs, Press Information Bureau release on Hyderabad Liberation Day, 17 September 2022, historical account of Operation Polo, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Failed negotiations, internal opposition and Razakar violence converged in a crisis, followed by Operation Polo and the Nizam’s surrender.
pictures.caption: Hyderabad's integration followed unsuccessful negotiations, internal unrest and military intervention.

title: Hyderabad: The Nizam, Razakars and Operation Polo
